transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Tesla's Third Quarter 2026 Q&A Webcast. My name is Travis Axelrod, Head of Investor Relations, and I'm joined today by Elon Musk, Vaibhav Taneja, and a number of other executives. Our Q3 results were announced at about 3:00 p.m. Central Time in the update deck we published at the same link as this webcast. During this call, we will discuss our business outlook and make forward-looking statements. These comments are based on our predictions and expectations as of today. Actual events or results could differ materially due to a number of risks and uncertainties, including those mentioned in our most recent filings with the SEC. Before we jump into Q&A, Elon has some opening remarks. Elon?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Thank you. The third quarter was very strong, and I'd like to give a big congratulations to the whole Tesla team for working hard to make it happen. Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It's exceeding our production by a significant margin. Obviously, we're going to be ramping, and we are ramping production meaningfully. The biggest driver for demand is full self-driving. Today, there's really no competitor for FSD in any car that you can buy. To be clear, we are producing and delivering as many cars as we can, and we're pushing very hard for FSD approval in additional markets. We're now approved in many countries in Europe, and we're hoping for EU-wide approval. It's hard to predict, but maybe within a few months. I would be surprised if it takes longer than Q1. Obviously, that's not a time frame we control, but we do anticipate being fully approved throughout Europe and in many other countries. We also began production of the Tesla Semi truck in Q3 and did the new Roadster demo, which was, I think, one of the most exciting events. Arguably, the coolest demo of any product ever, and that's a testament to amazing work by the Tesla and SpaceX teams. We've also been laying the groundwork for a lot more manufacturing capacity. I think we're aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030, and I think we've got a good shot at achieving that goal. Energy demand is very strong. We're actually almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027, and we're ramping production as quickly as possible to meet demand. We also expect gross margins on that to increase meaningfully. In a nutshell, after many years of a sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth. Regarding Robotaxi, we're seeing the fully autonomous miles driven scale exponentially, meaning they're scaling very rapidly. It would be hard to overstate this point. There really is extremely fast week-over-week growth in autonomous miles. I don't think there's any company in the world that can match our scale with autonomous vehicles as we continue to ramp. The Cybercab fleet in Austin, for example, has grown by a factor of 10 since launch about a month ago. The cumulative mileage is really—when I look at the weekly chart, it's wow. It looks like a rocket going to orbit, basically; it's growing very fast. I recommend that if you want to try it out, come to Austin and you'll see Cybercabs in use at scale, as I think a lot of people saw with the Austin City Limits concert recently. This is really going to a very good place. Regarding Optimus, we've started what I'd call early production on our high-volume line in Fremont. I want to elaborate on this point because I've said before that the growth of Optimus is an S-curve, but the initial part of the S-curve has a shallow slope and is somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product. The way to think about it is that there are about 10,000 things that have to go right for production of the robot, and it will move as fast as the slowest, least likely of those 10,000. We do have the vast majority of a 1-million-unit-per-line production line landed in Fremont right now. I would expect it to take us probably at least a year, maybe a little longer, to get to that annualized rate of 20,000 units a week. This is fundamentally because there are still parts of the design that are changing. A lot of people ask me about Optimus. That's why I think I've got to belabor this point a little: if people don't understand new technology or volume production of complex new hardware that well, it sort of seems like, 'Can't you just make a whole bunch of these things immediately and send them out?' No, you've got to basically build up an entire gigantic global supply chain and have a very, very big factory domestically, and everything has got to work. There are still some things we need to tweak about the design because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration. It can't wear out after a month. There's still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks. But, like I said, I would expect the AI, the electromechanical design, reliability, and duration—the usage life of the robot—to be solved around the end of next year. That's the time to expect when we're delivering Optimus to companies outside of Tesla. I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on Earth, and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on Earth. Optimus is a very big deal, but I don't want to temper expectations that we still have a lot to get through, and it'll take about a year or so to get through all that stuff. To the best of my knowledge, there is no one even close to Tesla with respect to a general-purpose humanoid robot. Regarding the Terafab, the Austin-based research fab is progressing quickly. We'll begin commissioning machinery in the first half of next year. Hopefully, if things go well, we'll make our first test chip just to see if we can make any chip at all around May or June. That's pretty exciting. Our aspiration is to be making some kind of useful chip at volume around Q3 of 2028. As I said publicly, I think the Terafab will be the most valuable building in the world and will probably have an economic value that will place it in the top 20 of countries. It's an epic project. This will be an incredibly important asset, if not a necessary asset, in order to scale, especially Optimus, as we can address bottlenecks in semiconductors, whether it's memory, packaging, logic, or whatever the case may be. With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday, tap-dancing through a minefield there. That's it. In conclusion, we're super excited about our autonomy and robotics road map. There's a lot of incredibly awesome stuff coming. I'd like to once again thank the Tesla team for their strong execution and all of our supporters for joining us on this journey.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thanks very much, Elon. Vaibhav has opening remarks as well. Vaibhav?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Thanks, Travis. We continued our progress on a lot of fronts in Q3. Elon already covered a lot of them. Additionally, I'd like to add that we also started deliveries of Megapacks with our in-house LFP batteries. We also had two consecutive quarters of vehicle deliveries over 480,000 for the first time. On the automotive business, we exited the quarter with our highest backlog in four years, with deliveries constrained primarily by production. We are therefore focused on increasing production at all our factories to meet this growing demand. While we are actively working to increase production, it does take some time to get every aspect dialed in, from supply chain to manufacturing to delivery logistics. The Model Y continued to outperform in the quarter and set delivery records in several key markets. Based on the preliminary data we've gathered, we believe that it was the number-one-selling BEV in Europe and the number-one-selling passenger car in South Korea. We also set new records in key markets, including Australia, Japan, and Taiwan. As Elon said, FSD continues to be the key driver for demand. In Q3, over 75% of deliveries in North America included a sign-up for a paid FSD subscription at the time of delivery, which is approximately 20% higher than Q2. Overall, the FSD attach rate continued to improve, reaching over 1.7 million paid customers globally, of which, for the first time, 50% are based on subscriptions. Given the strength of FSD in the U.S., we are taking extra steps to sell certain cars in Europe with some benefits to try and get more feet out there before broader FSD approval is obtained. On automotive margins, excluding credits, they increased sequentially from 16.3% to 18.1%. The improvement in margins is driven by a higher mix of deliveries in APAC. While commodity price increases and interest rate changes continue to add to our costs and create further headwinds, we have adjusted the vehicle financing programs to partially offset those costs. On the energy business, we had our second-best quarter of deployments, with 13.7 gigawatt-hours of energy storage. Energy gross margins improved from 20.4% to 33.1%. The sequential margin improvement is primarily attributed to tariff refunds recognized in the quarter and warranty true-downs resulting from alignment with our vendor on certain cell-related costs to be reimbursed by them. As Elon said, the business is witnessing extreme demand from data centers, and we are doing our best to increase production. Accordingly, we'll see improvements in ASP and further improvements in margins as we move forward. Services and other margins improved sequentially from 14.1% to 15.9%, an all-time high. This was the result of strength across several of the businesses in services and other, including Supercharging and insurance. The Robotaxi business, which is part of services and other, continued to grow with the launch of Cybercab rides in Austin. Cumulative unsupervised miles grew eightfold in the quarter, as we had weekly double-digit growth throughout the quarter. We're taking all the learnings from our Austin expansion to help us prepare for a broader Cybercab launch in other markets. Our priority is progressing the density and expansion of the network through vehicles that provide the best experience, like the Cybercab. We will also continue to augment the fleet with other variants over time to address the terrestrial transportation needs of the total population. I'd like to stress that what we are trying to do is literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation. We're starting with getting people from one place to another, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth. We are in a huge investment cycle to set us up for the future. Therefore, as previously guided, operating expenses continue to increase sequentially. Most of the increase came from significant research and development-related activities, including self-driving development costs, such as depreciation from additional compute, chip development, and preproduction ramp costs for new products like Optimus, Megapack 3, and the Semi truck. This trend of growing OpEx would continue until we commercialize these new products. Net income was impacted by a mark-to-market reduction of our SpaceX holding of $142 million, which was offset by a Bitcoin mark-to-market gain of approximately $290 million. We continued our efforts to manage cash efficiently and responsibly. We ended the quarter with positive free cash flow of over $1.5 billion and an overall cash and investment balance of over $45 billion. We're revising our CapEx guidance to be approximately $20 billion for the current year as a result of managing our capital deployment efficiently, and we plan to fund it primarily from our cash flows from operations. Additionally, during the quarter, we secured capacity to borrow up to $30 billion to support the expected growth in CapEx. Our confidence in the cash-generation capacity of our business and the investments we are making drove our decision to secure shorter-term financing. We don't plan to make any draws under any of the new facilities in this calendar year. The money that we received from the tariff refunds is being reinvested to expand production capacity in the U.S. I'd like to stress that we like to do a lot of hardcore, real grunt work to get production facilities up and running. Our CapEx for the next few years would continue to expand as we add more Robotaxi fleet, expand our production capacity for Optimus, install manufacturing capacity for solar, purchase additional self-driving compute infrastructure, and build a semiconductor fab. This strategy will position the company for the next era of growth and disrupt many existing markets while creating new ones. This is by far the most exciting time to be at Tesla. The foundation being laid around autonomy, robotics, and energy is setting us up for an extremely bright future. I would like to end by thanking the Tesla team, our customers, investors, and suppliers for their confidence in us on this journey.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Fantastic. Thank you, Vaibhav. Now we're going to go to questions from Say. The first question is: How does the Cybercab fleet scale past Austin, and what's the regulatory path outside Texas given NHTSA's Open Safety Review? Ashok, do you want to take that?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: Yes, I'll start here. First of all, we launched Cybercab this quarter, which is very exciting. We achieved that mostly by learning from data from the other vehicle platforms, for example, Model Y, Model 3, et cetera. All of that data helped us make the Cybercab without requiring a ridiculous number of vehicles to produce the data. So we are seeing very good scaling in terms of Cybercab's AI capabilities. We launched in Austin, but that's only because we had some cabs and we want to swarm Austin with Cybercabs everywhere. There's no fundamental reason that we are limited to Austin. In fact, next month, we'll be launching in Dallas, and then the same software will scale to lots of other cities along with the Model Y Robotaxis.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thanks very much. The next question is: What are your thoughts on crowdsourcing training data for Optimus versus your internal Optimus Academy approach? Is data currently the primary bottleneck? I think you covered this quite a bit, but any other color there?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: I mostly talked about this already, but crowdsourcing is not the issue for Optimus. There are a lot of things we have to get right about the AI architecture that we're still working on. We're making good progress, but that needs to be sorted out. Really, in order for Optimus to get the training data we need, we actually need to make a lot of Optimus robots. So we need to make, I think, on the order of 10,000 or 20,000 bots and then have them do self-play. We're building up an Optimus Academy where Optimus can practice doing a very wide range of tasks. Then we can use that data in a sort of flywheel to make it better and better at these various tasks. A big difference with Optimus versus the cars is that we don't have this vast fleet of cars from which we can gather training data. With Optimus, we have to bootstrap it by making the robots and having them do self-play, which is really how a human learns to navigate the world. You can see this when you have a toddler and they grow up. Initially, they're sort of wobbly and they don't know how to do things, and eventually they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone, as anyone who's had kids knows. Then they learn to read and do all sorts of things and be able to do these things. They learn this by playing. We actually need Optimus to play at scale in order for it to be really good at tasks in the real world. Ashok, you may want to add to that.

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: Yes. Like I mentioned, Elon, for the car, we actually have the data from the car's embodiment itself. But for Optimus, there's no exoskeleton for humans to get into and make Optimus into a puppet or something like that. We have to learn—Optimus has to learn by watching other people do tasks initially and then start practicing the tasks itself. For example, if you're watching a soccer game, just because you're watching, it doesn't mean you'll be good at soccer yourself. You've got to start practicing, get good at the game, and learn from the bot's own experience. We are setting up this huge reinforcement-learning cycle, with initial base training done from humans to bootstrap, and then putting it on Optimus and doing a lot of self-play, both in simulation and in the real world, to learn on the embodiment of Optimus itself. I think we're pretty close to having very good results in this big loop.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Yes. I think we may be ready to release an Optimus video in a month or so. I want to make sure that when we release this video, it's not a canned demo. When you see these humanoid robot demonstrations, some of them look very impressive, but they're not really using any kind of advanced AI or superintelligence. They're preprogrammed deterministic tasks. If you actually try to use that humanoid robot in the real world, you would have a lot of trouble. It wouldn't work, basically. So I want to release a video where Optimus is doing things that are not preprogrammed. I think it may be a month or two before we have a demo where you can believe what you see. Then there's another milestone that's important for us to reach, which is to integrate our Tesla AI5 chip into Optimus. If things go according to plan, that will be in approximately April of next year. That's a giant improvement in capability, with an order of magnitude more operations per second—an order of magnitude more compute, AI5 versus AI4. That will help Optimus a lot because the degrees of freedom that a humanoid robot has to deal with are far greater than what a car has to deal with. It is a bit of a struggle to squeeze in everything needed to operate with all the degrees of freedom of Optimus and the wide range of tasks. You can think of a humanoid robot as doing something like 1,000 times more things than a car would do. That's some very big number, basically. I think the additional compute of AI5 will make a big difference, and that comes in, hopefully, in volume around April of next year. That's why I think all the pieces—the refinements in electromechanical dexterity, making sure Optimus can operate for long periods of time without wearing out, getting the AI software right, and integrating the AI5 chip—kind of come together. That's why I think about a year from now is when it's something that you could ship to customers. It would also be reaching scale in production. That's probably the right timing to think about. In terms of the initial customers for Optimus, I think it probably would be industrial applications at first: dangerous, repetitive tasks, things that people really don't want to do and that you want done basically 24/7, around the clock. That's going to be the highest value for Optimus in the beginning. As we scale production, of course, it would be something that people can buy for their home. But the initial high-value use will be—the highest-value use, I think, will be heavy industry, dangerous tasks, or things that may cause repetitive stress injuries and that you want done 24/7. That's the way to think about it.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thank you, guys. The next question is very similar. It's about Optimus scaling, so we can go past that one.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: I just answered that one, basically.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: The next question is: When can we anticipate FSD unsupervised in customer cars? Ashok, do you want to kick that off?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: Yes. Like I mentioned earlier, the software for Cybercabs and Model Y is the same, and pretty soon we'll be able to release the same software as part of the v15 release to customers. The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer's Model Y can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous. We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the Robotaxi fleet.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thank you, Ashok. The next question is: When will the Cybercab be available for customer purchase or ownership? Lars, did you want to kick this one off?

transcript.speaker: Lars Moravy
transcript.title: Vice President of Vehicle Engineering
transcript.content: Sure. Thanks, Travis. I think it builds a little bit on what Ashok just said. In short, we're trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026. Obviously, we're producing them on our line in Texas, but all of those are currently going to our own internal Robotaxi fleet. As Tesla grows, we'll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers, and Cybercab will be the first. As we start small this year and learn about all the things Ashok mentioned about delivery, ownership, and fleet management of autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we'll continue to scale that. Elon, I don't know if there's anything you want to add to that?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: No. Cybercab is primarily going to be something that is offered as transport as a service, whereas our other cars would be more the cars that you'd want to own, like the 3 and the Y and whatnot, and Roadster, obviously. The vast majority of the Cybercab fleet will essentially be Tesla-owned and transport as a service.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thanks, guys. The next two questions are quite similar around unit economic costs. The first one is on per-paid Robotaxi mile, and the second one is cost per Optimus unit. We already covered what the first paying customer looks like. Vaibhav, did you want to get into the unit economics question here?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. On the Robotaxi side, in the main geographies where we are operating, we're already seeing utilization improving. Week by week, as Elon was talking about, we look at the miles and how many paid rides are happening. Are we at our goal of $0.30 today? No. But do we see a path to get to that? Yes, we do. It's all about scaling operations. What you'll see over the next few months is that today Cybercab, which is the primary Robotaxi product, is available only in Austin, but we do plan to bring it out in some other cities before the end of this year. As we add more Cybercabs, we're also learning from the operational experience of managing a fleet: pickup and drop-off, cleaning, all those things. All those costs are being dialed in. That's why, like I said before, we definitely see a path to get to our $0.30 target.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: And then did you want to cover the Optimus costs?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. I think Optimus cost internally is tracking pretty well in terms of how the design has matured. But it would be a little too early to say that we've got there because, as Elon was saying, we're still making a lot of design iterations. The good thing is, when you look at it from a cost perspective, we're trending closer to where we would say our Cybercab costs would end up being.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thank you very much, Vaibhav. The next question is, when do you—we've kind of already answered this—when do you anticipate Optimus will be generating revenue? We covered that in the prior question. The next one is: Mapping for FSD continues to be a problem. The three biggest issues are recognizing proper speed limits, parking, and typical routes. I understand you use various third-party maps, but why not use your own maps? Authorized, trusted, and verified Tesla owners could provide the input. Ashok, did you want to kick off here?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: Yes. You're totally right that we shouldn't be depending on external people's maps. We are building our own maps, but not in the same way as OpenStreetMap. We are building an entirely new architecture with essentially AI-based mapping and navigation. It's going to be super awesome. It's going to be integrated with voice. You can talk to it and ask for different routes. It's going to learn your personalized preferences, plus the fleet preferences. The collective intelligence of all the cars is going to flow into making the maps and navigation super cool. We'll start—you'll see the start and end of trips already use this technology pretty soon as part of the v15 release. Over the next several months, it's just going to take over all of the navigation functions: parking, destination handling. It will know you better than you know yourself in some regard for the driving task, and then handle it fully.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thank you, Ashok. Our last question is: What is the current production rate at your existing factories? Do you anticipate building new ones? Lars, do you want to kick that off?

transcript.speaker: Lars Moravy
transcript.title: Vice President of Vehicle Engineering
transcript.content: Yes, sure. I think Vaibhav touched a little bit on this in his opening remarks. I'll say our factories are operating at record rates this quarter. Of course, they can only build at the rate of the least lucky process or component. Vaibhav mentioned that we are actively managing all aspects of production. As we've spoken about in our past calls, we've made strategic investments globally to increase rates at our current factories over the last year-plus. This quarter, we are starting to see that, and we expect it to continue in coming quarters as those investments come to fruition. Beyond that, we've also been working to ramp Cybercab, obviously, in Giga Texas, and we've applied for the proper permits to expand the factories in Berlin. As Elon also mentioned, we just started our new Semi factory in Reno. In short, we are building new factories, yes, and we're aiming to hit that 5-million goal by 2030, as Elon said.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Thank you very much. That's it for the Say questions. Now we will be going to analyst questions. As a reminder, as Elon said, we will not be addressing any questions today on a potential merger with SpaceX. The first question comes from Tom from RBC.

transcript.speaker: Gautam Narayan
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: It's on FSD. The attach rate, according to my math, is like 30% to 40% in North America on a paid basis. It's becoming a flywheel, as you said, for more car sales, and the attach rate exceeds other automakers' subscription-based autonomy by a lot. In a weird way, could you guys be a victim of your own success, with other carmakers noting the success and trying to aggressively come up with similar L2+ type products, maybe partnering with NVIDIA or Qualcomm? If that happens, could that be deflationary for FSD pricing?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: I think people take this very simply: that you can—if the software can be solved, it's not because—I mean, I'll let Ashok get into it. But basically, it's a very hard problem.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Super hard problem.

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: Yes, it's easy to get to the first 90% and make a cool-looking demo. But when you get into the long tail of this problem, it's so long that people don't realize anyone in their sane mind should not attempt to solve this problem. It's so difficult and such a long tail. Especially getting to a safety point where you can drive safely for millions of miles with no injuries and so on is going to be extremely hard. As we release unsupervised FSD to the broader customer fleet, I don't think anyone can match it for several years.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: One other thing I'll say, if it wasn't clear: especially in our showrooms here in the U.S., customers are now coming in and saying, 'Can we get into an FSD drive?' They're not asking for 3, Y, or Cybertruck. They're saying, 'Can we get an FSD drive?' That has become the key driver because what it does is actually open up a lot more flexibility for different parts of the population who had issues driving conveniently before. Now they're getting their freedom back by being able to use FSD. A lot of folks are just like—I mean, it's a game changer. If you haven't tried it, I keep saying it every time: if you do, you won't be able to go back to driving any other car.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Tom, do you have a follow-up?

transcript.speaker: Gautam Narayan
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Yes. The follow-up is similar to that question on China. There, it seems like autonomy is table stakes. Is it the same kind of answer as question one—that those carmakers aren't going to be able to develop similar products to your FSD? Or do you see a definitely different pricing dynamic there?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: At the beginning, definitely, the leapfrog we have in terms of this technology isn't there with any of the other Chinese OEMs today. We're working very diligently to try and get broader FSD approval in China. It is hard, but for certain cars, we have been able to have FSD operating. Whoever has tried it there understands how much better it is compared with any of the competition. In fact, I don't know if you've seen this, but there have been some competitor CEOs who have come and done FSD drives here in the U.S., and they themselves have been blown away by what FSD is capable of doing. So it is a similar answer. Again, we're not taking it lightly. We're actively working with the regulators in China because, I don't know if you saw this, but we released our safety report on FSD before, and we've also released our unsupervised Robotaxi safety report. We think this is the right way to get people into a safe environment, because you know the number of accidents that happen because drivers aren't alert. This is the only way we can ensure that there are fewer casualties in the world, and any regulator who looks at the data would find it very hard to refute.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Our next question comes from Emmanuel from Wolfe.

transcript.speaker: Emmanuel Rosner
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: On Robotaxi, you've talked about sustaining double-digit week-over-week growth in unsupervised miles. I'm curious if there's a way you can triangulate that for us into revenue and maybe profitability of the Robotaxi business. If you sustain, let's say, 15% week-over-week growth in these miles, you'll probably cross 10 million miles by the end of the year. How many miles would you need to generate gross profit?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: I think Elon talked about this a little bit at the beginning: using exponential math, this would become a significant part of our revenue and profitability in '27.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Yes. I wouldn't say it's going to move the needle this quarter. But I think it starts to become noticeable probably in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Emmanuel Rosner
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Got it. If I think about it in terms of fleet size, I think your Cybercab line capacity is listed at more than 125,000 units a year. Production just recently started. How do you expect the ramp-up curve to be on the Cybercab line?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: I'll kick it off, but then I'll also let Lars chime in. I would give kudos to the engineering team. They have designed a product—because not only do I talk to the engineers, I also talk to the manufacturing guys—and they think this is one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing. So scaling would not be that much of a challenge. I think the key thing we're trying to make sure of is that we have all the regulatory approvals so we can start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them. Lars, feel free to chime in.

transcript.speaker: Lars Moravy
transcript.title: Vice President of Vehicle Engineering
transcript.content: Yes. Thanks, Vaibhav. I appreciate the accolades. The team definitely crushed it on the Cybercab design and manufacturing. To your point, we have 50% fewer parts than any other vehicle we've ever built. That's 50% fewer things to go wrong. We've definitely been bursting the Cybercab line to see how fast we can run it. I think the listed capacity is more of a rate at which we're capable of running today, but the actual capacity of that vehicle line is significantly higher. Right now, we're building at the rate that the Robotaxi service needs the vehicles. I'll say Ashok and I are in a bit of a race to see who's going to stay ahead. He's got exponential growth coming on the miles month over month, and we're going to look to meet that as well with vehicle production.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. The next question is going to come from Andrew from Morgan Stanley.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Percoco
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: I want to start on your energy business. You're clearly seeing a lot of demand on the energy storage or Megapack side, and you've got some goals to bring on your own solar manufacturing. I was hoping to get a little more insight into how you're thinking about Tesla's role in enabling both distributed power and distributed compute. I think last quarter you alluded to a Megapod product. I'm hoping to get a little more insight into what you're envisioning there and ultimately how big this could be for Tesla.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: I think it's still early days on that front. We don't know the full extent of how that will unfold. I think we'll have a better sense for that probably at the end of Q1 or in Q2. It does have a lot of potential. It's just hard to say how much potential right now.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Percoco
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay. Understood. Maybe just a follow-up on Robotaxi. It does seem like you've hit an inflection point here in Austin over the last month or so since you launched the Cybercab. Would you generally say that the bottlenecks to growth at this point are more regulatory-driven as you think about expanding into new geographies, and that you've gotten through most of the hurdles on the software side? I'm curious how you would generally categorize some of those growth hurdles in the incremental regions you're planning on scaling into over the next few months.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: I think there are still certain software challenges that we're working through. Ashok talked about it. So maybe Ashok, you can...

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: I'll chime in. For example, we initially had the Robotaxi service from 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., and then we expanded to 10:00 p.m., 11:00 p.m. Now it's going to be pretty soon 2:00 a.m. So we are slowly expanding the availability of Robotaxi, and that is driven by the capability of the AI software. We just want to make sure that there's not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. Even if there's the slightest possible risk at all, we don't take on that risk. We are very risk-averse in that sense: we want zero injuries or anything bad happening, and that is the driving principle. Over the rest of this year, we'll unlock 24/7 operation and go to higher-speed roads. We think all of that is necessary to scale and offer a great product to a lot of users. That's why we wanted to do both breadth first, with multiple cities—we do six cities now—and depth, with a lot of vehicles in a single city, which is Austin. We'll expand to more weather conditions, day and night conditions, highways, and high speeds. All of that will hopefully be done by the end of this year, at which point you will see a lot more scaling and a lot more cities covered by Robotaxi. So it's not purely regulatory or something like that. It is technology-driven, but we do see that becoming regulatory pretty quickly, perhaps in Q1 or Q2 time frames.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. The next question is going to come from Edison from Deutsche Bank.

transcript.speaker: Xin Yu
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: First, I wanted to ask about Terafab. Elon, I know you mentioned an aspirational goal of Q2 '28. Do you have a sense of how much capital needs to be invested to get there? Also, what kind of milestones should we be on the lookout for along the way?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Well, it's going to be some pretty significant capital. It's certainly in the tens of billions for Terafab. We've got to figure out the relative split between SpaceX and Tesla in terms of who pays for what at Terafab. But it's not going to be less than tens of billions in capital equipment up through early 2028. Long term, it will probably be north of $100 billion.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. I'll just add that we've actually already placed most of the orders for the first set of equipment for the fab Tesla is building. That's why when Elon was talking about the middle of next year, that is from the first fab, which...

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: The research fab.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Research fab.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Yes. That's where we're just figuring out how to work the equipment, that type of thing. Real production would be late '28, which is lightning fast by fab standards.

transcript.speaker: Xin Yu
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Understood. Understood. A quick follow-up on Optimus. I know you mentioned that we could see a video soon and that there's quite a bit of progress, but you're still making some refinements. Generally speaking, where do you see most of the design changes still happening going forward? Is the hand still an issue? Anything you can call out there?

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Yes, it's most of the difficulty. Konstantinos, why don't you answer this question?

transcript.speaker: Konstantinos Laskaris
transcript.title: Executive
transcript.content: The hand is one of the most challenging hardware areas, actually. Most of the electromechanical system, I would say, is relatively high confidence, meaning that it has converted to something that works decently well. The hand, from an electromechanical point of view, is more complicated than actuators for the locomotion system, for example. There are also some bespoke gears that are carrying a lot of burden for consumption and reliability that we are still developing. Yes, this would be the most...

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Yes. It's mostly the hand and just the fine-tuning of the hand design and the fingers, especially. It's a hard problem because humans have self-repair: our hands repair themselves; our bodies repair themselves, but robots don't. Our fingers are kind of squishy and have lots of sensors in our skin. It's hard to make a hand that can handle lots of wear and tear but is still squishy enough to pick up delicate objects, has all the sensors, and doesn't damage the sensors when you do repeated actions. There are a lot of little things that make you realize what an incredible thing the human hand is at the end of the day. From an electromechanical standpoint, it's mostly the hands. Other things are improving throughout the robot as well, but that's the main thing. Then, as I mentioned, upgrading the intelligence—the onboard intelligence of the robot—with AI5 is a big step change in intelligence that will help a lot with the capabilities of Optimus. I've said before that the usefulness of humanoid robots will be a rough approximation of the electromechanical dexterity, the AI software, and the AI chip hardware. All three of those things are improving exponentially. We use that word a lot, but the value is roughly those three things multiplied by each other. Then the Optimus robots will build future Optimus robots, so you have a recursive function. When you have a recursive, multiplicative exponential, things will really grow extremely fast. They may start from a small base, but they're going to grow to crazy levels. I think at some point there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. The next question comes from Alex from Bank of America.

transcript.speaker: Alexander Perry
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: First, on Robotaxi. It looks like you're pricing lower than competitor rideshare and other Robotaxi players in most markets. Is that the plan longer term, to take market share given some of your structural cost advantages?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. Remember, when you're comparing, you're comparing us with rideshare, which has a driver in there, and we don't. Plus, we manufacture the car ourselves, so our overall cost basis is different. I think I said it in my opening remarks, and I'll say it again. I don't want to be too repetitive, but basically, our goal is to take over any kind of transportation.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: I think unless we are stopped by governments, which is certainly a possibility if they're trying to protect the domestic industry, Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: You can come back and look at this prediction, but I feel confident about it.

transcript.speaker: Alexander Perry
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Really helpful. My follow-up question is on the key metric here, unsupervised miles driven. I think it grew at a high-teens weekly growth rate since late July. Is it still the expectation that you'll continue to grow that at a double-digit weekly rate through the balance of the year? What is really enabling that type of growth? It seems like you've definitely hit a comfort level and are scaling much more rapidly. How much of that is Cybercab? How much is better safety validation with the latest version of FSD? On fleet composition, do you expect Cybercab to represent a majority of the Robotaxi fleet over time?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.title: Vice President of Autopilot Software
transcript.content: Yes. We will continue the scaling for the foreseeable future. We don't see any hurdles along the way. Obviously, there's work required, but we do see a clear path toward scaling to millions of vehicles over the next several months. This is happening primarily because of the technology investments we have made over the last several years and also the v15 stack that we alluded to earlier this year. All of the foundations are hard to see. It's like an iceberg: people only see the tip of the iceberg. There's a ton of work that goes into it, and now we're starting to see the payoff of all that work—developing end-to-end neural networks, learning from humans, and so on. All of that is paying off. That's what you're seeing. You're seeing the result of many years of work; it didn't just happen in the last several months. The same technology should scale to millions of vehicles wherever we are allowed to operate.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Our next question is going to come from Pierre from New Street.

transcript.speaker: Pierre Ferragu
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: I wanted to come back to this. I'm really fascinated by 75% of U.S. cars selling with FSD. It makes a minimal impact on the numbers in the quarter the car is sold, but over the lifetime of the car it probably at least doubles the profit per car. Where I want to get to is: Am I looking at it the right way? Are you at some point going to disclose the annual recurring revenue that FSD represents? I did my own math, and I'm thinking it's probably now approaching $1 billion of ARR. Is that the right order of magnitude?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO

transcript.speaker: Pierre Ferragu
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay. As a quick follow-up, do you already have a good sense, and can you tell us about the retention rate? How many people, three or six months down the line, stick to the monthly subscription? Do you see a percentage of drivers falling off?

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO

Still, people are signing up even though that free subscription is available.

transcript.speaker: Travis Axelrod
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Great. Our next question is going to come from Colin at Oppenheimer.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Well, that's what we're doing. We're building robots that do not have perfected hands, and we're making progress with Optimus training and ironing out all aspects of the supply chain and the production system. All these things are happening simultaneously. We're growing as fast as humanly possible here. I don't think anyone is going to have—and, in fact, I'd be stunned if anyone has—a robot remotely competitive with Optimus when we start delivering it to customers, which is likely to be toward the end of next year.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. You should know that it's not only the Fremont factory. We've also started constructing a factory here in Austin, which would be able to make a lot more robots compared with the Fremont one. Going back to what Elon was saying, we're doing whatever we can. We're not stopping; we're just going at the fastest pace we can.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.title: CEO
transcript.content: Yes. We're definitely, as I say, in Vegas betting on the come.

transcript.speaker: Colin Rusch
transcript.title: Analyst
